entry.title: [ News ] Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of NVIDIA
entry.content:
NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has officially announced his resignation.

After 33 years as CEO of NVIDIA, Jensen Huang has announced that he will resign from the company that he co-founded. As both a husband and father of two adult children, Huang was revealed in recent weeks to have been having an affair with two separate women.

One affair was with Kimberly Powell, a long-time employee of NVIDIA and current vice-president of healthcare. She is a graduate of Northwestern University and an engineer. She previously worked within the company on applications for GPU computation in medical imaging.

The other affair was with a woman named Alice Huang (no relation). She is the CEO of the Singaporean firm called Megaspeed which is a direct customer of NVIDIA. Beyond merely being a conflict of interest and violation of NVIDIA corporate ethics, this affair is also being actively investigated by USA intelligence services. Alice Huang has been identified as being a potential spy working on behalf of the chinese government. The affair raises important questions about whether Beijing was attempting to procur access to restricted GPU exports, or gain information regarding the USA administration, for which Jensen had close ties.

Jensen Huang’s immediate replacement will be NVIDIA’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress. She will serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor can be determined.

entry.title: [ Trivia ] NVIDIA founder Jensen Huang is a relative of AMD CEO Lisa Su.
entry.content:
Jensen Huang was born in in 1963 in Taipai, Taiwan. At nine years old his parents sent him and his brother to live with their uncle in Tacoma, Washington. He was academically gifted, and after finishing public school would go on to study electrical engineering at Oregon State University. He then worked in chip design for Texas Instruments, LSI Logic, and even AMD before founding his own company NVIDIA in 1993. He and his co-founders would work together on their business plan while eating at their favorite Denny’s restaurant location.

Lisa Su was also born in Taiwan. At just three years old her family immigrated to the United States, settling in New York City. She had an early passion for engineering, demonstrated by taking apart her brother’s remote control cars to understand how they worked. She was given her first computer in junior high school, an Apple II which she taught herself how to use. She would obtain her master’s degree in electrical engineering from MIT in 1991. Later, she would go on to work for industry giants such as Texas Instruments (as Huang did) as well as IBM. For many years she would work as an engineer at AMD before eventually rising to become vice president of the company, and then finally CEO in 2014.

Both Huang and Su share a common ancestor, a man named Lo Chü. He is grandfather to Jensen, and great-grandfather to Lisa. This makes them first cousins once removed. They did not grow up together, and only met later in life after they had both established their careers.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jensen_Huang

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Su

Source: https://www.tomshardware.com/news/jensen-huang-and-lisa-su-family-tree-shows-how-closely-they-are-related

entry.title: [ News ] Tesla Cybertruck to be discontinued in 2027
entry.content:
Elon Musk has stated that Cybertruck production at the Texas Gigafactory will end in 2027.

In a status update to his personal X.com account, Tesla CEO Elon Musk announced that Cybertruck would no longer be produced at the Texas production facility.

The following is his direct quote.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

Cybertruck was only ever produced in that factory meaning this is the presumed end of this model line.

The truck was controversial. It had an unorthodox design which included a distinct steel-alloy exterior with very hard edges. It was launched at a higher price than Musk had originally claimed and had on-going issues related to build quality and safety.

I’ll be completely honest and admit that I liked the Cybertruck. I appreciated the retro-futurist design, and considered it to be a geeky ‘lifestyle’ truck similar to Hummers and G-Wagons.

entry.title: [ Trivia ] George Renninger, the 19th century confectioner is regarded as the original creator of Candy Corn.

He originally referred to his classic Autumn treat as ‘Chicken Feed’. It wouldn’t become popularly named Candy Corn until after World War 1, when the American diet began incorporating more corn-derived foods.

As one of its original producers, the Goelitz Candy Company (now Jelly Belly) helped to popularize the candy. They ran ad campaigns including one in which a bold rooster characture declares himself the “King of the Candy Corn Fields”.

In the modern era most Candy Corn is produced by Ferrero under the Brach’s brand. They control roughly 85% of the market. The National Confectioners Association has estimated that about 35 million pounds of Candy Corn are produced each year. They have also declared October 30th to be National Candy Corn Day.

entry.title: [ News ] Patrick Stewart has died
entry.content:
Actor Patrick Stewart has passed away. He was well known for his performance as Jean-Luc Picard on the TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation.

Born Patrick Hewes Stewart on July 13 1940 in Yorkshire England, he had a life-long acting career in which he performed many popular roles. While best known for his on-screen performances he was also a well-recognized stage actor, having become a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966.

On-screen he was perhaps best known for his role as the Captain Jean-Luc Picard on the TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation. He also performed as Professor Charles Xavier in the very popular Marvel’s X-Men series of films.

In politics Patrick Stewart was outspoken and actively supported social equality, labour rights, and civil liberties. He was an atheist and a patron of the secular humanist charity Humanists UK.

Patrick Stewart died of Alzheimer’s disease in Los Angeles on Wednesday October 28, 2026.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Stewart

entry.title: [ Trivia ] The term ‘Computer Bug’ was popularized by programmer Grace Hopper after she removed a moth from a malfunctioning computer.
entry.content:
In 1947, acting as a lieutenant junior grade for the US Navy Grace Hopper was assigned to the Bureau of Ships Computation Project. The project was using the Harvard Mark II computer to perform ballistics calculations among other things. After encountering a malfunction in the computer Hopper and her team discovered that a moth had gotten stuck on one of the machine’s relays and was the ultimate cause of the fault. This amusing detail would later be included in her team’s notes.

Using ‘bug’ to refer to a fault or malfunction in a machine pre-dates Grace Hopper’s use of the word, but she is often credited with popularizing the word for use by programmers. In modern software development fixing incorrect codes is often called ‘debugging’, and a tool that helps to identify bad codes is called a ‘debugger’.

Source: https://www.vassar.edu/grace-hopper/achievements

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Hopper

entry.title: [ Trivia ] Phineas Gage was a 19th century American man who survived an iron rod piercing his skull.
entry.content:
As a young man Gage was a construction worker under contract with the Rutland and Burlington Railroad company. On September 13, 1848 the 25 year old Gage was on the line when his tamping rod was accidentally fired upward by a gunpowder fuse, at very high speed. With his head directly in the rod’s path, it pierced his skull and continued to fly a long distance behind him.

To the surprise of his doctors, Phineas Gage both survived the initial injury and was both coherent and able to speak to them. In a matter of months he was recovered enough to return to work.

He lived for another 12 years after the incident, and in that time he was reported to have had a significantly changed personality. He had become more impulsive and quick to anger. Eventually he would die of a seizure while working as a stagecoach driver in Chile.

The incident is known as the “American Crowbar Case”, and became the subject of academic research and discussion throughout the 19th century. It posed important questions related to the functioning of the brain, and the nature of consciousness.

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phineas_Gage

Source: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Phineas-Gage

entry.title: [ Trivia ] Among all species Humans are one of the best at long-distance endurance running.
entry.content:
<style>
    /*
     * A 3D runner, drawn as nothing but its outline: a skinned mannequin (Quaternius'
     * Universal Animation Library, CC0, stripped down to runner.glb beside this file)
     * running in place. It's rendered in two passes: the runner's normals and depth go
     * to an off-screen buffer, then an edge-detect shader draws only where those jump
     * (the silhouette, overlapping limbs and creases) in the site's accent colour.
     * The gait is set in the script (GAIT: jog, sprint, or a blend between them).
     * Drag to turn the view.
     *
     * three.js (with its glTF loader and meshopt decoder: runner.glb is
     * meshopt-compressed) is vendored beside this file as three-gltf.min.js and only
     * fetched, along with the model, once the figure comes near the screen.
     * The outline follows the theme's accent colour.
     *
     * Until then, and instead of it without JavaScript or WebGL, a still frame of
     * the same view stands in: runner-fallback.webp, a capture of the render kept
     * as just its alpha, used as a mask over the accent colour so it follows the
     * theme too.
     */
    #hrun {
        --hrun-slide: 2em;
        --hrun-fade: .9s;

        margin: 1.5rem auto;
        max-width: 40rem;
    }

    .hrun-stage {
        position: relative;
        aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
        touch-action: pan-y;
        cursor: grab;
        user-select: none;
    }
    .hrun-stage.hrun-dragging { cursor: grabbing; }
    .hrun-stage canvas { display: block; width: 100%; height: 100%; }

    /* the still frame: shown until the 3D view is in, and instead of it if that fails */
    .hrun-still {
        position: absolute;
        inset: 0;
        background-color: var(--color-primary);
        mask: url("runner-fallback.webp") center / contain no-repeat;
        pointer-events: none;
    }
    /* nothing to drag without the 3D view */
    .hrun-stage.hrun-static { cursor: auto; }

    .hrun-credit {
        margin-top: .5rem;
        text-align: center;
    }
    .hrun-hint { display: block; }
    .hrun-hint[hidden] { display: none; }

    /*
     * Intro, like the family tree's (trivia 10): the stage fades in and drops into
     * place with a strong ease-out once the model has loaded and is on screen.
     * !important: the page column's `.animate-on-hover:hover *` would otherwise swap
     * in its short default while the pointer is over the post.
     */
    #hrun .hrun-stage canvas,
    #hrun .hrun-still {
        transition:
            opacity var(--hrun-fade) ease,
            transform var(--hrun-fade) cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) !important;
    }
    #hrun .hrun-pre { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(calc(-1 * var(--hrun-slide))); }
    /* the still frame fades out in place as the 3D view comes in */
    #hrun .hrun-still.hrun-gone { opacity: 0; transform: none; }

    @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
        #hrun .hrun-stage canvas,
        #hrun .hrun-still { transition: none !important; }
    }

    @media (max-width: 640px) {
        .hrun-stage { aspect-ratio: 4 / 3; }
    }
</style>

<!-- The stage gets its canvas from the script; the still frame stands in until then. -->


<script type="module">
    "use strict";

    // ── Tuning ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    /** The model, beside this file in the page bundle. */
    const MODEL_URL = new URL("runner.glb", location.href).href;

    /** The vendored three.js build (three + GLTFLoader + MeshoptDecoder only). */
    const THREE_URL = new URL("three-gltf.min.js", location.href).href;

    /**
     * The two gaits, as the clips in runner.glb. `metres` is how far the root moves
     * over one loop, read from the root-motion version of the library (UAL1_Standard_RM):
     * the floor slides back at metres / duration, so the feet stay planted.
     */
    const GAITS = [
        { clip: "Jog_Fwd_Loop", metres: 5.0 },
        { clip: "Sprint_Loop",  metres: 5.5 },
    ];

    /**
     * Playback speed of the run: 1 = real time, 0.5 = half speed. Scales the stride
     * and the floor together, so the feet stay planted at any value.
     */
    const SPEED = 0.5;

    /** The gait: 0 = jog, 1 = sprint; in between blends the two into one stride. */
    const GAIT = 0;

    /** Where the camera sits: distance from the runner's hips, height, and field of view. */
    const CAMERA = { distance: 4.5, height: 1.8, target: 0.65, fov: 30 };

    /** The view's starting angle around the runner, in degrees (0 = side on); dragging turns it from there. */
    const VIEW_START = -35;

    /**
     * The outline: `width` is the line's thickness in CSS pixels; `crease` is how sharp
     * a fold in the surface must be to draw (0–1 of normal change; lower draws more),
     * and `depth` how big a jump in distance, relative to the nearer surface, counts as
     * one part passing in front of another.
     */
    const OUTLINE = { width: 0.75, crease: 0.35, depth: 0.04 };

    /**
     * The floor: a grid in the outline's colour and width, of square tiles `tile` metres across,
     * clipped to a circle of `radius` metres around the runner whose last `fade`
     * metres fade out, drawn at `opacity` so the runner stays the brighter line.
     */
    const FLOOR = { tile: 0.6, radius: 1.4, fade: 0.7, opacity: 0.5 };

    // ── Page ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    const root    = document.getElementById("hrun");
    const stage   = root.querySelector(".hrun-stage");
    const still   = root.querySelector(".hrun-still");
    const hint    = root.querySelector(".hrun-hint");

    const reduced = window.matchMedia("(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)").matches;

    /**
     * Gives up on the 3D view: the still frame stays, and the stage stops offering a drag.
     * @param {string} why What went wrong (for the console).
     * @param {unknown} [err] The error, if there was one.
     */
    function fallBack(why, err) {
        console.warn(`running.html: ${why}; showing the still frame`, err ?? "");
        stage.classList.add("hrun-static");
        stage.querySelector("canvas")?.remove();
    }

    /**
     * Resolves a CSS colour (the site's are oklch, which three can't parse) to sRGB
     * by painting it: a 1×1 canvas reads back whatever the browser makes of it.
     * @param {string} css Any CSS colour, `var(--x)` included.
     * @returns {[number, number, number]} 0–1 sRGB channels.
     */
    const resolveColor = (() => {
        const probe = document.createElement("span");
        const ctx = document.createElement("canvas").getContext("2d", { willReadFrequently: true });
        return css => {
            probe.style.color = css;
            root.append(probe);
            const computed = getComputedStyle(probe).color;
            probe.remove();
            ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 1, 1);
            ctx.fillStyle = computed;
            ctx.fillRect(0, 0, 1, 1);
            const [r, g, b] = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 1, 1).data;
            return [r / 255, g / 255, b / 255];
        };
    })();

    // ── Scene ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

    /**
     * Builds the scene, loads the runner and starts it. Called once the figure is
     * near the screen, so nothing heavy is fetched for readers who never get here.
     */
    async function start() {
        const THREE = await import(THREE_URL);

        let renderer;
        try {
            renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ alpha: true });
        } catch {
            fallBack("no WebGL");
            return;
        }
        // A shader that won't compile on this GPU: say why, and keep the still frame.
        let shaderError = null;
        renderer.debug.onShaderError = (gl, program, vs, fs) => {
            shaderError = [gl.getProgramInfoLog(program), gl.getShaderInfoLog(vs), gl.getShaderInfoLog(fs)]
                .filter(Boolean).join(" | ").replace(/\0/g, "").trim() || "unknown";
            console.error("running.html: shader error:", shaderError);
        };
        // Supersampled: edge detection can't use the canvas's own antialiasing, so draw
        // at twice the screen's density and let the browser's downscale smooth the lines.
        renderer.setPixelRatio(Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio * 2, 3));
        renderer.setClearColor(0x000000, 0);
        renderer.domElement.classList.add("hrun-pre");
        stage.prepend(renderer.domElement);

        const scene  = new THREE.Scene();
        const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(CAMERA.fov, 1, 0.1, 50);

        // Pass 1: the runner's view-space normals (as colour) and depth, off screen.
        // Where nothing is drawn the alpha stays 0 and the depth at the far plane.
        const target = new THREE.WebGLRenderTarget(1, 1, {
            depthTexture: new THREE.DepthTexture(1, 1),
        });
        const normalMat = new THREE.MeshNormalMaterial();

        // Pass 2: a full-screen quad that compares each pixel of pass 1 with its four
        // neighbours (`width` pixels away) and draws the accent colour where the normal
        // turns sharply or the depth jumps; transparent everywhere else.
        const outlineMat = new THREE.ShaderMaterial({
            uniforms: {
                tNormal:  { value: target.texture },
                tDepth:   { value: target.depthTexture },
                uStep:    { value: new THREE.Vector2() },
                uColor:   { value: new THREE.Color() },
                uCrease:  { value: OUTLINE.crease },
                uDepth:   { value: OUTLINE.depth },
                uNear:    { value: camera.near },
                uFar:     { value: camera.far },
                // the floor: the camera (by reference, so always current), the line
                // width in buffer pixels, how far the grid has slid, and FLOOR
                uInvProj:  { value: camera.projectionMatrixInverse },
                uCamWorld: { value: camera.matrixWorld },
                uCamPos:   { value: camera.position },
                uLineW:    { value: 1 },
                uScroll:   { value: 0 },
                uFloor:    { value: [FLOOR.tile, FLOOR.radius, FLOOR.fade, FLOOR.opacity] },
            },
            vertexShader: /* glsl */ `
                varying vec2 vUv;
                void main() {
                    vUv = uv;
                    gl_Position = vec4(position.xy, 0.0, 1.0);
                }`,
            fragmentShader: /* glsl */ `
                #include <packing>
                uniform sampler2D tNormal, tDepth;
                uniform vec2 uStep;
                uniform vec3 uColor;
                uniform float uCrease, uDepth, uNear, uFar;
                uniform mat4 uInvProj, uCamWorld;
                uniform vec3 uCamPos;
                uniform float uLineW, uScroll;
                uniform vec4 uFloor;  // tile, radius, fade, opacity
                varying vec2 vUv;

                /** Distance from the camera at uv (the far plane where the runner isn't). */
                float dist(vec2 uv) {
                    return -perspectiveDepthToViewZ(texture2D(tDepth, uv).x, uNear, uFar);
                }
                /** The surface normal at uv, back from 0–1 colour to -1–1. */
                vec3 normal(vec2 uv) {
                    return texture2D(tNormal, uv).rgb * 2.0 - 1.0;
                }

                float d0;
                vec3 n0;
                float jump, crease;

                /** Compares the neighbour at uv with the centre, keeping the biggest change. */
                void neighbour(vec2 uv) {
                    float d = dist(uv);
                    jump = max(jump, abs(d - d0) / min(d, d0));
                    crease = max(crease, 1.0 - dot(n0, normal(uv)));
                }

                void main() {
                    // (four plain calls, not an array in a loop: some mobile drivers mishandle those)
                    d0 = dist(vUv);
                    n0 = normal(vUv);
                    jump = 0.0;
                    crease = 0.0;
                    neighbour(vUv + vec2(uStep.x, 0.0));
                    neighbour(vUv - vec2(uStep.x, 0.0));
                    neighbour(vUv + vec2(0.0, uStep.y));
                    neighbour(vUv - vec2(0.0, uStep.y));
                    // creases only count on the runner (the empty background has no normal)
                    float onRunner = step(d0, uFar * 0.99);
                    float edge = max(
                        smoothstep(uDepth, uDepth * 2.0, jump),
                        onRunner * smoothstep(uCrease, uCrease * 1.5, crease)
                    );

                    // The floor: where this pixel's view ray meets the ground (y = 0),
                    // a grid line there, clipped and faded around the runner, and
                    // hidden wherever the runner is nearer. (No early return: fwidth
                    // needs every pixel to run the same code.)
                    vec4 farPt = uInvProj * vec4(vUv * 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0);
                    vec3 rayView = farPt.xyz / farPt.w;
                    vec3 ray = (uCamWorld * vec4(rayView, 0.0)).xyz;
                    float down = step(ray.y, -1e-4);
                    float t = -uCamPos.y / min(ray.y, -1e-4);
                    vec3 hit = uCamPos + t * ray;
                    vec2 cell = vec2(hit.x, hit.z + uScroll) / uFloor.x;
                    vec2 px = abs(fract(cell - 0.5) - 0.5) / fwidth(cell);  // pixels to the nearest line
                    float line = clamp(uLineW * 0.5 + 0.5 - min(px.x, px.y), 0.0, 1.0);
                    float circle = 1.0 - smoothstep(uFloor.y - uFloor.z, uFloor.y, length(hit.xz));
                    float shown = step(-t * rayView.z, d0);  // the floor is nearer than the runner (or no runner)
                    float floorA = down * line * circle * shown * uFloor.w;

                    float a = max(edge, floorA);
                    gl_FragColor = vec4(uColor * a, a);  // premultiplied, onto a clear canvas
                }`,
            depthTest: false,
            depthWrite: false,
            blending: THREE.NoBlending,
        });
        const screen = new THREE.Scene();
        screen.add(new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.PlaneGeometry(2, 2), outlineMat));
        const screenCam = new THREE.OrthographicCamera(-1, 1, 1, -1, 0, 1);

        /**
         * Picks up the theme's accent colour. The shader writes it straight to the
         * canvas, so it goes in as plain sRGB, outside three's colour management.
         */
        function applyPalette() {
            const [r, g, b] = resolveColor("var(--color-primary)");
            outlineMat.uniforms.uColor.value.setRGB(r, g, b, THREE.LinearSRGBColorSpace);
            requestFrame();
        }

        // ── The runner ──

        let gltf;
        try {
            gltf = await new THREE.GLTFLoader().setMeshoptDecoder(THREE.MeshoptDecoder).loadAsync(MODEL_URL);
        } catch (err) {
            fallBack("the model failed to load", err);
            return;
        }
        const runner = gltf.scene;
        runner.traverse(obj => {
            if (!obj.isMesh) return;
            obj.material = normalMat;
            obj.frustumCulled = false;  // the skinned pose strays outside the bind-pose bounds
        });
        scene.add(runner);

        // Both gaits play at once, weighted by the blend; neither advances on its own
        // (timeScale 0): each frame sets their times from one shared phase, so the
        // blend between them is always mid-stride in both.
        const mixer = new THREE.AnimationMixer(runner);
        const gaits = GAITS.map(g => {
            const clip = THREE.AnimationClip.findByName(gltf.animations, g.clip);
            const action = mixer.clipAction(clip);
            action.setEffectiveTimeScale(0).play();
            return { action, duration: clip.duration, metres: g.metres };
        });

        // ── State ──

        const blend = GAIT;
        let phase = 0;           // 0–1 through the stride
        let scroll = 0;          // metres the floor has slid back
        const playing = !reduced;  // with reduced motion: a still pose
        let azimuth = THREE.MathUtils.degToRad(VIEW_START);
        let visible = false;
        let frameId = 0;
        let dead = false;        // gave up: the still frame stays
        let last = performance.now();

        /** Puts the camera on its circle around the runner, at the current angle. */
        function placeCamera() {
            camera.position.set(
                Math.sin(azimuth + Math.PI / 2) * CAMERA.distance,
                CAMERA.height,
                Math.cos(azimuth + Math.PI / 2) * CAMERA.distance,
            );
            camera.lookAt(0, CAMERA.target, 0);
        }

        /** Poses the runner for the current phase and blend. */
        function pose() {
            for (const [i, g] of gaits.entries()) {
                g.action.time = phase * g.duration;
                g.action.setEffectiveWeight(i === 0 ? 1 - blend : blend);
            }
            mixer.update(0);
            outlineMat.uniforms.uScroll.value = scroll;
        }

        /**
         * One frame: advances the stride and the floor by the time since the last, then
         * draws in two passes: normals and depth off screen, then the outline found in
         * them, with the floor.
         * @param {number} now The frame's timestamp (ms).
         */
        function frame(now) {
            frameId = 0;
            const dt = Math.min((now - last) / 1000, 0.1);
            last = now;

            if (playing) {
                // The blended stride: its length and its time, so speed = metres / seconds.
                const seconds = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(gaits[0].duration, gaits[1].duration, blend);
                const metres  = THREE.MathUtils.lerp(gaits[0].metres,   gaits[1].metres,   blend);
                phase = (phase + SPEED * dt / seconds) % 1;
                scroll = (scroll + SPEED * dt * metres / seconds) % 1000;
            }
            pose();
            placeCamera();
            renderer.setRenderTarget(target);
            renderer.render(scene, camera);
            renderer.setRenderTarget(null);
            renderer.render(screen, screenCam);
            if (playing && visible) requestFrame();
        }

        /** Asks for a frame (just one at a time). */
        function requestFrame() {
            if (!frameId && !dead) frameId = requestAnimationFrame(frame);
        }

        /** Fits the canvas to the stage. */
        function resize() {
            const { width, height } = stage.getBoundingClientRect();
            if (!width || !height) return;
            renderer.setSize(width, height, false);
            const px = renderer.getDrawingBufferSize(new THREE.Vector2());
            target.setSize(px.x, px.y);
            const step = OUTLINE.width * renderer.getPixelRatio();
            outlineMat.uniforms.uStep.value.set(step / px.x, step / px.y);
            outlineMat.uniforms.uLineW.value = step;
            camera.aspect = width / height;
            camera.updateProjectionMatrix();
            requestFrame();
        }
        new ResizeObserver(resize).observe(stage);

        // Only animate while on screen.
        new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
            visible = entries.some(e => e.isIntersecting);
            last = performance.now();
            if (visible) requestFrame();
        }).observe(stage);

        // Drag sideways to turn the view (vertical drags still scroll the page on touch).
        let dragX = null;
        stage.addEventListener("pointerdown", e => {
            dragX = e.clientX;
            stage.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
            stage.classList.add("hrun-dragging");
        });
        stage.addEventListener("pointermove", e => {
            if (dragX === null) return;
            azimuth -= (e.clientX - dragX) * 0.01;
            dragX = e.clientX;
            requestFrame();
        });
        const endDrag = () => {
            dragX = null;
            stage.classList.remove("hrun-dragging");
        };
        stage.addEventListener("pointerup", endDrag);
        stage.addEventListener("pointercancel", endDrag);

        // Follow the theme: light / dark is an attribute on <body>, the hue a style on
        // <html>. Read again once the site's 0.5s colour transition has finished too.
        const repaint = () => { applyPalette(); setTimeout(applyPalette, 550); };
        new MutationObserver(repaint).observe(document.body, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-dark-mode"] });
        new MutationObserver(repaint).observe(document.documentElement, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["style"] });

        // ── Go ──

        applyPalette();
        resize();
        frame(performance.now());

        // Check the first frame actually drew something before swapping out the still
        // frame: read the canvas straight back (still valid within this task).
        const gl = renderer.getContext();
        const px = new Uint8Array(gl.drawingBufferWidth * gl.drawingBufferHeight * 4);
        gl.readPixels(0, 0, gl.drawingBufferWidth, gl.drawingBufferHeight, gl.RGBA, gl.UNSIGNED_BYTE, px);
        let drawn = 0;
        for (let i = 3; i < px.length && !drawn; i += 4) if (px[i]) drawn++;
        if (shaderError || !drawn) {
            dead = true;
            fallBack(shaderError ? `shader error: ${shaderError}` : "the first frame came out blank");
            return;
        }

        requestAnimationFrame(() => {
            renderer.domElement.classList.remove("hrun-pre");
            still.classList.add("hrun-gone");
            still.setAttribute("aria-hidden", "true");
            hint.hidden = false;
        });
    }

    // Fetch three.js and the model once the figure is close to the screen.
    if ("IntersectionObserver" in window) {
        const near = new IntersectionObserver(entries => {
            if (!entries.some(e => e.isIntersecting)) return;
            near.disconnect();
            start().catch(err => fallBack("the 3D view failed", err));
        }, { rootMargin: "300px" });
        near.observe(root);
    } else {
        start().catch(err => fallBack("the 3D view failed", err));
    }
</script>
<p>A noteworthy ability of the Human species is to run for long, uninterrupted periods of time.
Few species are better, and Humans are the only ape that is capable of it.</p>
<p>Among many others, specific traits which enable this include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Taller body with more surface area which facilitates evaporative cooling (sweating)</li>
<li>Wider heel bone to better absorb impact</li>
<li>Longer legs enabling a greater stride</li>
</ul>
<p>It is an ability that likely evolved in conjunction with <a rel="noopener external" target="_blank" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persistence_hunting">Persistence Hunting</a>,
a technique which involves chasing an animal over long distances. The Human hunter can withstand the chase better than their prey, and eventually
they will catch it even if initially the animal can run faster. If the hunter can keep chase long enough, the prey animal will either
succumb to exhaustion, overheating or injury.</p>

entry.title: [ Trivia ] The Pygmalion Effect is a psychological phenomemon in which placing high expectations on someone leads to their better performance.
entry.content:
The Effect is an example of a self-fulfilling prophecy, the subject of the expectation performs better because of their belief that their performance is required, and not merely an optional choice.

The Pygmalion Effect is named for the sculptor Pygmalion from greek mythology. In his story he crafts a statue, and falls so intensely in love with his creation that it transforms into a real woman.

The term was coined by psychologists Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacombson. They conducted a study on school children in which the teacher expressed both high and low expectations on the students. As measured by IQ test scores, children who were expected to perform well had higher scores. Conversely, children who were expected to perform poorly by their teachers had lower scores.

entry.title: [ Blog ] The Algoma Programming Language
entry.content:
Here’s the big project that I’ve been working on for the past few months.

Algoma is my own personal programming language. I started working on it earlier in the year, and I’ve been building it from scratch in C++. I followed along with the book called Crafting Interpreters by Robert Nystrom. It’s an excellent read and I highly recommend it if you are interested in programming language implementation and/or design.

I followed along in Nystrom’s book to implement the basic features. I chose to use the design from the later chapters: a single-pass compiler and virtual machine. I’ve since moved on from the book, and have started to implement my own features. I don’t yet have a proper specification for the language, and likely won’t have one for a while. Right now I’m just adding and tweaking features to suit my taste, or even just to experiment. I want to maintain that design freedom for the foreseeable future, and otherwise just have fun with it.

If I’m being honest, I don’t feel as though I have progressed enough to start demonstrating my work publically. Yet I have been growing increasingly frustrated with my pace towards a working demo.

So I’ve decided to just throw what I have so far onto the internet, for all to see. It’s not ready yet by my measure, but it is something at least. It’s a working build of the graphical user interface that has a bit of functionality available now to start playing around with. Click the big button below to check it out.

entry.title: [ News ] Fully autonomous drones have killed human soldiers for the first time
entry.content:
A military contractor named Alexander Kokhanovskyy has revealed that a test was conducted two years ago in which fully autonomous drones killed human soldiers.

The test involved sending ‘terminator’ drones on a trajectory over several kilometers towards their target. Upon arrival an AI running on the drones identified and then engaged their target. Human-piloted drones flew over the area some time afterwards to confirm the targets had been eliminated.

The Ukrainian government presently requires final human confirmation to conduct attacks, but otherwise uses AI heavily in identifying targets. Kokhanovskyy claims there has been no further tests beyond the one conducted two years ago.

Kokhanovskyy is currently the CEO of Aero Center, a Ukrainian military drone manufacturer. Aero Center is a new company, and was not responsible for conducting the test.

In my opinion this was inevitable and was going to happen eventually. It’s still not too late to impose a global ban on these types of weapons, but before that happens I expect to see more stories like this.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Swiss Chalet Dipping Sauce
entry.content:
This is a copycat recipe for Swiss Chalet Chicken Sauce that I tried recently. It’s very good, and very rich. I liked the taste, but I think I used too much sage. If you try this for yourself make sure to follow the recipe exactly.

Ingredients

  • 🐄 4 tbsp Butter
  • 🌽 3 tbsp Corn Starch
  • 🐔 3 cups Chicken Broth
  • 🍅 1/4 cup Tomato Juice
  • 🍷 1 tsp White Vinegar
  • 🧅 1 1/2 tsp Onion Powder
  • 🌿 1 1/2 tsp Paprika
  • 🍀 3/4 tsp Dried Sage
  • 🧄 1/2 tsp Garlic Powder
  • 🧂 1/2 tsp Table Salt
  • 🌻 1/2 tsp Dried Summer Savory
  • 🫚 1/4 tsp Ginger Powder
  • 🌿 1/4 tsp Mustard Powder
  • 🍀 1/4 tsp Thyme
  • 🥬 1 Bay Leaf

Instructions

  1. In a medium sized saucepan, melt butter over medium heat.
  2. Allow to cook, whisking frequently, until it begins to brown.
  3. Add corn starch, whisk until smooth.
  4. Slowly add chicken broth, whisk constantly to fully incorporate with butter.
  5. Add remaining ingredients, continue whisking.
  6. Turn heat to medium-high, then bring to a boil.
  7. Turn heat down to low and simmer for 5 minutes.
  8. Remote bay leaf, serve hot.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Why I'm Grateful Today
entry.content:
Today I am grateful for this website, lzon.ca. I started building it about a week ago, and so far I am quite satisfied with it, at a technical level.

I’m using the Zola static site generator. I started from scratch, without a template. I wanted to improve my web development skill, and I wanted a challenge. There was a moment on day one in which I literally had an empty index.html file loaded in my text editor.

The name is a contraction of the word “Lauzon”, pronounced “loh-zawn”. It’s the name of a lake near Blind River, Ontario. My Mom was born there and otherwise it is a very nice little town, in a part of the province that I love. The domain was also surprising inexpensive.

I think the design of the site is nice so far, and I’ve already learned a few new things related to web development and design:

  • A new trick for addressing FOUC
  • How to create advanced CSS selectors
  • New ways to use CSS variables

I don’t know now how frequently I will publish content to this site. At the very least it can be a place to publish my rambles, when I feel compelled. Either way, I am satisfied with what this is right now.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Twenty Twenty-Five
entry.content:
The year is almost over.

“How is it November already?”

“Where did the time go?”

I’ve heard it, you’ve heard it, and probably felt it too. I haven’t felt it much at all, at least not recently. 2025 has been a year, a whole year, by my reckoning.

Unemployed

It’s been nearly a year since my previous post, since I was feeling grateful. I did in fact lose my job. It was at the end of February, and it wasn’t surprising. I feel I handled it well initially, or at least regarded my unemployment with appropriate seriousness. I immediately got to work: I updated my resume, my professional website, and even attempted to register a business. I did well to keep myself motivated. I know very well the rot that creeps into a person when they are unemployed for too long, and beyond anything else I was motivated to prevent that from happening.

I’ve submitted several dozen applications this year. By some standard, that no longer exists, that might have been a lot (or at least an appropriate amount). I realize fully that by modern standards it is not nearly enough. I haven’t had a single follow up, and of course no interviews.

I struggle in the extreme with feelings of judgement, and I always have. It makes job applications difficult, especially when I am taking them seriously. A few of my applications were for jobs I genuinely wanted, and it hurt when I didn’t even get a response. Many times I intentionally applied to jobs I didn’t care for, or otherwise was barely qualified, just to tell myself that I was trying.

It starts creeping back

What is creeping? I think the best single word for it is merely ‘despair’. Deep despair, deeper that I ever thought possible before I felt it. Complete, and fully internalized hopelessness. I was being consumed by it before finding my job, and by summer this year I was beginning to feel it again.

The thinnest of silver linings is that I saw it coming. The despair is here again. I wasn’t able to stop it, but I have (so far) discovered ways to live with it. To not let it destroy me.

Not that I actually care anymore about my future. I wake up every day on a mission:

  • At 6:50am, every day, I get out of bed.
  • I exercise. Hard, for 1 hour.
  • I attend to my hygeine, and the tidyness of my living space.
  • I go to my computer and begin working. On anything. If my progress on any given project begins to stall, I panic, and grab desperately for something else to do. I force myself to believe that working on these projects counts as ‘productivity’.
  • I go out to buy groceries in the afternoon, and eat a single meal, my supper, at 6pm.
  • My energy is mostly spent by the evening, and I can’t even enjoy a video game. So most days I do nothing until going to bed.
  • In general, I don’t sleep well.

I have become ridgidly attached to my schedule. I panic whenever it is disrupted (e.g. eating supper 30 minutes later than usual), because it represents stability. It’s my flimsy defense against chaos. Its predictable and reliable. I really don’t like living this way, but I know that if not for this, my life would be so much worse.

The Motorcycle

In early summer I was consistently becoming stalled on all of my projects. Lingering panic was setting in, and after doom scrolling Marketplace my brain began to latch on to the idea of buying a motorcycle. I’m sure a part of me was genuinely excited by the prospect, but my attitude was ultimately fatalistic. I wanted a motorcycle because learning to ride was ‘something to do’, ‘anything to do’. I also was genuinely happy for the possibility of a dramatic (and quick) death if I had a crash. What happens next feels like punishment from the universe for daring to hope that I could be put out of my misery quickly and cleanly.

The Broken Foot

I rode the bike for 1 week. Then, at a complete stand-still, I lost my balance. The bike fell, with me under it, and my foot was crushed.

Multiple bones were broken, others were fractured. I was put into a cast that evening, and thus began the next 8 weeks.

By all outward appearances, I must have seemed to be taking it well. I had exactly two outbursts, which I intentionally allowed myself to have. I shouted, and stomped (with my walker). Beyond that, I did not complain much at all.

I maintained my schedule, I never missed a workout. I modified my stationary bike to accomodate the cast, and continued to ride. In a very real sense I was acting out of spite to the universe, for having done this to me. I did everything in my power to prevent it from disrupting me.

Overall, I feel I was genuinely more content during this time than I was before, and now. It felt justified to let go of my concerns about my life trajectory, at least for a while. I’ve tried to maintain this mindset after I began walking again, but unsurprisingly that hasn’t happened. I can feel the weight of the future again. It feels heavy, opaque, and threatening.

11:51AM

It’s almost noon. I haven’t completed a notable task yet on any of my projects. I’ll scramble to get something done, to alleviate the anxiety.

Most years seem to go by quickly, especially as you get older. For me, 2025 has felt like a whole-ass year.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Pollo Sabrosa
entry.content:
This is a recipe that I came up with. I had some leftover rice one day and wanted something meaty, spicy, and flavorful to throw on top. I have already made this several times before writing it down.

The result was very dense and filling, and was very nice as leftovers for several days after. The name ‘Pollo Sabrosa’ is Spanish for ‘Tasty Chicken’.

The following recipe is based on my memory. It probably isn’t exactly right, but this is simple enough that it shouldn’t make a huge difference.

Ingredients

  • 🐔 2 lbs ground chicken
  • 🐔 1 lbs boneless chicken breast or thigh
  • 🐔 2 cup chicken broth
  • 🫑 2 Bell Pepper, chopped
  • 🌶️ 3 jalepeno peppers, chopped
  • 🧅 2 large onions, chopped
  • 🧅 1 garlic bulb, chopped
  • 🌶️ 250 g chili powder (at least 1 packet, depending on the brand)
  • 🚬 2 tbsp liquid smoke
  • 🌿 2 tbsp black pepper
  • 🍀 2 tbsp oregano
  • 🌱 2 tbsp red pepper flake

Instructions

  1. Saute onion and garlic in a large stove-top pot.
  2. Cut whole chicken cuts into medium-sized chunks, then add them to pot. Add ground chicken as well.
  3. Add peppers, liquid smoke, and broth. Then stir on medium-high heat until mostly cooked.
  4. Add dry spices. Continue to stir on medium heat until done.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Barb's Beef Stroganoff
entry.content:
My Mom’s Beef Stroganoff recipe.

Ingredients

  • 🐮 4 tbsp butter
  • 🧅 1 chopped onion
  • 🧄 4 cloves minced garlic
  • 🍄 1 lb sliced mushrooms
  • 🐄 beef cubes seasoned with salt and pepper
  • 🌿 2 tsp Dijon mustard
  • 🍀 1 tsp paprika
  • 🍷1/3 cup dry white wine
  • 🐄 2 cup beef broth
  • 🍞 2 tbsp flour
  • 💮 1 tbsp Worcestershire sauce
  • 🧂 salt and pepper (to taste)

Instructions

  1. Cook beef in the butter.
  2. Then cook the onions, cloves, mushrooms.
  3. Mix in the mustard and paprika.
  4. Add the wine, cook 5 mins.
  5. Mix beef broth, flour, Worcestershire sauce, until smooth.
  6. Pour beef broth mixture into the pan, mix well and bring to a simmer, until thick.
  7. Add cream cheese at the end. (do not boil)
  8. Add noodles at the end.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Barb's Bodacious Banana Bread
entry.content:
My Mom’s banana bread recipe.

Ingredients

  • 🍞 2 cups all purpose flour
  • 🧑‍🍳 1 1/2 tsp baking powder
  • 🧑‍🍳 1 tsp baking soda
  • 🧂 1/2 tsp salt
  • 🍬 1 1/2 cups granulated sugar
  • 🐮 1/2 cup butter
  • 🐄 1/4 buttermilk
  • 🍌 3 or 4 mashed bananas
  • 🥚 2 large eggs
  • 💮 1 tsp vanilla extract

Instructions

  1. Combine flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large mixing bowl.
  2. Add sugar, butter, buttermilk and bananas.
  3. Beat on medium speed for 2 minutes.
  4. Add eggs, vanilla and another 1/4 cup buttermilk
  5. Beat on medium speed for 1 minute.
  6. Spread batter evenly in 2 greased 9“ pans.
  7. Bake at 350° F for 30-40 minutes.
  8. Cool 10 minutes, then remove from pans and cool completely, spread frosting.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Baked Lemon Pepper Pork
entry.content:
Another riff on my original Baked Cajun Pork recipe. I’m writing this recipe the day after I cooked the meal, so I might have forgotten specific measurements. I’ll update if neccessary.

Be careful when adding both the lemon pepper and mustard, these are both very high sodium and otherwise powerful flavors (don’t use too much).

Ingredients

  • 🐖 2 - 3 lbs of your preferred cuts of pork (1 or 2 grocery store packages)
  • 🫙 1/3 cup liquid smoke
  • 🍋 1/3 cup lemon juice
  • 🌿 1/3 cup mustard
  • 🍋 2 tbsp lemon pepper spice (1 tbsp for marinade, 1 tbsp dusted on top)
  • ☘️ 2 tbsp parsley (1 tbsp for marinade, 1 tbsp dusted on top)
  • 🍅 tomato (fresh or canned)

Instructions

  1. Into a large bowl, mix together liquid smoke, lemon juice, mustard, lemon pepper.
  2. One at a time, marinade the pork cuts in the bowl, then place them flat in a baking tray.
  3. Dust parsley and lemon pepper onto the pork cuts.
  4. Top the pork cuts with tomato, to your preference.
  5. Place in an oven for a minimum of 60 minutes at 350° F. Cook longer and hotter if desired (I usually cook for 75 minutes at 400° F, which makes the pork slightly crispy).

entry.title: [ Blog ] Jollof Seasoning
entry.content:
A standalone ingredient list for the Jollof Seasoning used in my Baked Jollof Rice recipe. The flavor is unique and earthy, and not too hot. I used it originally for rice and chicken. It works well as a general purpose spice, I’ve used it for pork, and turned it into a dipping sauce.

This recipe produces a large quantity of seasoning, make sure you have a large container for storage.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Gratitude
entry.content:
Today is another decent day. The shop is just busy enough: I have enough to do that I don’t feel un-needed but I’m also not overworked.

For the second time this month I was told to stay home for lack of work to do. I understand fully, and agree that it was warranted, but this has rattled me none-the-less. Before now I have always had a consistent schedule. I was told 45 minutes before closing that I wouldn’t be working the following day. This took me by surprise, and I feel that I should have been given more notice.

Either way, I feel that I responded appropriately. I acknowledged the situation politely and professionally. The following day I immediately began searching for job postings, and updating my resume. I in no way want to lose this job, and I have recieved no indication yet that I’m in danger of losing it. But this is yet another very stark reminder that my position is precarious.

In recent years, I’ve gotten a lot better at appreciating the present moment, not dwelling too much on the past, or future. I’ve gotten better at feeling gratitude for the nice things immediately in front of me, such as meaningful and interesting work.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Precarity
entry.content:
I’m having a decent day today. The shop is quiet. I haven’t done much but I don’t feel completely useless either.

*** wanted to go to an event with his family and my being here allowed him to do that, or at least made it easier for him to do so.

A previous customer came in asking for help gaining access to her email. She is by no means unintelligent, but is genuinely tech illiterate. I had resolved her issue in under five minutes, and did not charge her for the service. We spoke at length about a possible upgrade to her old desktop computer at home. I won’t know for sure until next year if she is truly interested, but it seems likely.

During my performance review my boss said plainly, “I don’t need another person in the shop”. By this he meant that he was expecting me to work with his business clients: maintaining network infrastructure, responding to support requests, etc… He knew when he hired me that I was not immediately qualified to be doing these things, and that I’d have to learn while I was working. I have been genuinely trying to learn, but clearly that effort has thus far been insufficient. He hasn’t told me with any detail what his expectations are, only that I have not been meeting them. It has been weeks since that performance review and nothing has changed. I continue to work in the shop, and try to work on peronsal projects that will develop skills that might be useful in my work.

I feel I have no choice but to regard my situation as fundamentally precarious. The Sword of Damocles is swinging constantly over my head. Some days I can see it more clearly than others. Today it is less visible, fortunately.

This post began with instances of what I feel is genuine usefulness. Going forward I want to make sure that I am grateful for them. It is during those moments that I like this job. They also reinforce my belief that I have competancy, and that I have something that I can offer to others.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Baked Jollof Rice
entry.content:
I took my old Baked Beans & Rice recipe and modified it using this Jollof Rice recipe I found from Ethan Cheblowski.

The result was fantastic. I served this with BBQ chicken for a meal, using some of the spice mix on the chicken. I still had plenty of leftover spice mix, which I will definitely be using again.

The standalone recipe can be found here.

Ingredients (Spice Mix)

  • 🫚 4 tbsp ground ginger
  • 🌿 4 tbsp thyme
  • ☘️ 2 tbsp coriander
  • 🧅 2 tbsp onion powder
  • 🧄 1 tbsp garlic powder
  • 🌱 1 tbsp cinnamon
  • 🌶️ 1 tbsp red pepper flakes
  • 🌿 1 tbsp paprika
  • 🐔 1 tbsp chicken broth powder
  • 🧂 1 tbsp salt
  • ☘️ 1/2 tbsp nutmeg

Ingredients (Sauce)

  • 🍅 4 tomatoes
  • 🫑 2 bell peppers, chopped
  • 🌶️ 2 jalepeno peppers, chopped
  • 🧄 1 bulb of garlic, chopped
  • 🌿 2 tbsp curry powder
  • ☘️ 6-8 tbsp jollof spice mix

Ingredients (Rice)

  • 🍚 2 cups rice
  • 🧅 2 onions, chopped
  • 🫑 1 bell pepper, chopped
  • 🥤 1 cup water
  • 🧈 2 tbsp butter, melted
  • 🧂 2 tbsp M.S.G. (optional)

Instructions

  1. Preheat oven to 350 ℉ (175 ℃).
  2. Add together the spice mix, and set aside in a sealable container. There will be leftovers.
  3. Using a blender (or your preferred cooking appliance), blend together the sauce ingredients until smooth. Set aside.
  4. Into a large cooking tray, add rice and almonds. Pour melted butter over the rice/almonds and stir until everything is evenly coated.
  5. Pour the sauce over the rice, then the cup of water, then add the chopped onions and bell peppers. Stir everything until well mixed.
  6. Cover the tray, with a lid or aluminium foil.
  7. Bake in oven for 60 - 70 minutes. Optionally serve with sour cream and green onion garnish.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Baked Cajun Pork
entry.content:
A very easy and simple weeknight-style meal, made from scratch. I also make a Curry Pork of this recipe with a potent Indian-style flavor.

Ingredients

  • 🐷 2 - 3lbs of your preferred cuts of pork (1 or 2 grocery store packages)
  • 🫙 1/3 cup liquid smoke
  • 🫙 2/3 cup Worcestershire sauce
  • 🌿 3 tbsp Cajun Seasoning
  • 🧅 1–2 medium-sized onions, or other miscellaneous veggies

Instructions

  1. Chop the veggies (I like to slice the onions into thick rings).
  2. In a large baking tray, lay down veggies as a bed.
  3. Into a large bowl, mix together liquid smoke, Worcestershire sauce, and Cajun seasoning.
  4. One at a time, marinade the pork cuts in the bowl, then place them over the veggie bed.
  5. Place in an oven for a minimum of 60 minutes at 350° F. Cook longer and hotter if desired (I usually cook for 75 minutes at 400° F, which makes the pork slightly crispy).

entry.title: [ Blog ] Creamy Garlic Pasta
entry.content:
This is one of the earliest recipes that I learned. It is meant to mimic the flavor of Knorr Sidekicks pasta mix.

It tastes amazing, and is very rich and filling. I don’t make it much anymore since it isn’t particularly nutritious.

Ingredients

  • 🥛 1/4 cup powdered milk (4 tablespoons)
  • 🌽 2 tablespoons corn starch
  • 🧂 1 teaspoon salt
  • 🌿 1 teaspoon parsley
  • 🧄 3-4 diced garlic cloves
  • 🧅 1-2 diced onions
  • 🧈 4 tablespoons butter
  • 🥤 4 cups cold water
  • 🥣 seashell pasta, or preferred variety

Instructions

  1. Add dry ingredients, garlic, onion, butter, and water to a medium-sized saucepan.
  2. Stir in pasta until saucepan is full, ensuring that all noodles are fully submerged.
  3. Simmer on medium heat until pasta is tender. Stir frequently.
  4. Optionally, serve with grated Parmesan.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Baked Beans & Rice
entry.content:
This is one of the first recipes I learned when I started to cook. It’s simple, cheap, filling and nutritious. It’s also very flexible: I’m constantly riffing on this recipe, and I’ve never made a bad batch.

Ingredients

  • 🍚 3 cups rice, basmati or preferred variety
  • 🧂 2 teaspoons salt
  • 🌿 1 teaspoon black pepper
  • ☘️ 2 teaspoons ground cumin
  • 🌶️ 1 tablespoon chili powder
  • 🥵 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper (optional)
  • 🌿 1/4 teaspoon oregano
  • 🫒 1/4 cup olive oil (4 tablespoons)
  • 🍅 1 jar tomato salsa (16 ounces)
  • 🐔 2 cups chicken or beef broth
  • 🫘 2 cans black beans, rinsed and drained (15 ounces each)
  • 🧅 2 large chopped white onions

Instructions

  1. Preheat oven to 350 ℉ (175 ℃).
  2. Pour rice into a casserole dish and season with salt, pepper, cumin, chili powder, cayenne, and oregano. Pour in olive oil and stir until rice is thoroughly coated with oil. Add salsa, broth, onions and beans; stir until evenly combined. Cover very tightly with aluminum foil
  3. Bake until rice is tender, about 1 hour 10 minutes. Remove foil, taste and adjust seasoning if necessary, and fluff with a fork. Serve hot, optionally garnish with green onion.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Beef Stroganoff
entry.content:
Just a standard Beef Stroganoff recipe. I’ve made it a few times and everyone always likes it.

Ingredients

  • 🐄 3 lbs beef
  • 🍷 1 1/2 white wine
  • 🐮 2 cups beef broth
  • 🥛 1/4 cup table cream
  • 🥛 3/4 cup sour cream
  • 🧅 2 onions
  • 🧄 2 cloves garlic
  • 🍄 8 oz mushroom

Instructions

  1. Cut beef into thin strips
  2. Cook on high heat until thoroughly browned, with a careful amount of olive oil.
  3. Remove beef from pot, cook mushroom, onion, and garlic in the beef fat.
  4. Deglaze with white wine, add broth once bottom is clean.
  5. Add beef back to the pot, simmer for 10–20 minutes.
  6. Add the creams, then add a thickener (flour) as desired.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Black Bean Burgers
entry.content:
Another recipe that I only ever tried once. I liked it, but it was otherwise unpopular in my house. It’s vegetarian but not vegan-friendly (it uses egg as a binder).

They are very dense and filling.

Ingredients

  • 🧅 1/2 large red onion, chopped
  • 🌶️ 1-2 whole chipotle peppers in adobo sauce (optional)
  • 🫘 2 cans black beans drained and rinsed (15 ounces each)
  • 🍞 1 cup plain bread crumbs
  • 🌿 1 1/2 teaspoons cumin
  • 🧂 3/4 teaspoon salt
  • 🧄 4 cloves garlic
  • ☘️ 1/2 teaspoon black pepper
  • 🥚 2 large eggs

Instructions

  1. Place onion, chipotle, and garlic into a food processor and pulse until finely chopped. Add black beans and pulse until beans are partially chopped, leaving some whole or partial beans. Transfer to a large mixing bowl.
  2. Stir in bread crumbs, cumin, salt, pepper and eggs until well combined.
  3. Divide mixture to for 8 patties.
  4. When ready to cook choose one of the following options:
    • Fried: Heat a lightly oiled skillet to medium high heat. Cook for 5 minutes on each side.
    • Baked: Bake in a 400 ℉ oven for 5 minutes each side.
    • Grilled: Cook on an outdoor grill for 5 minutes each side.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Gingerbread
entry.content:
I only tried this recipe once. It turned out nice, but it wasn’t interesting enough for me to try it again.

Ingredients

  • 🐮 1 cup (237 mL) milk or water
  • 🍫 1/2 cup (118 mL) molasses
  • 🍯 1/2 cup (118 mL) honey
  • 🧈 1/2 cup (one stick, 113g) butter
  • 🧂 1/2 cup (100g) granulated sugar
  • 🥚 1 egg
  • 🍞 2 1/2 cups (300g) all-purpose flour
  • 🧂 1/2 teaspoon salt (maybe 3/4 if using unsalted butter)
  • 🧑‍🍳 1 1/2 teaspoons baking soda
  • 🌿 2 tablespoons ground cinnamon
  • 🫚 2 tablespoons ground ginger (use half if you don’t want it very spicy)
  • ☘️ a little finely-ground black pepper

Instructions

  1. Heat oven to 350ºF/180ºC.
  2. Prepare a loaf pan with grease or parchment sling.
  3. Pour milk/water into a bowl, along with the molasses and honey.
  4. Drop in the butter in chucks. Microwave until butter is mostly melted.
  5. Put the flour in a mixing bowl with the salt, baking powder, and spices. Whisk to combine and fluff up the flour.
  6. Add the sugar to the wet ingredients along with the egg and stir. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry and whisk until smooth.
  7. Pour mixture into the loaf pan and bake for 1 hour.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Ginger Pork Stir Fry
entry.content:
A very tasty oriental-style meal. I don’t make it often, but it has been great every time I’ve made it.

Ingredients

  • 🐷 3 lbs pork tenderloin
  • 🥢 6 tbsp soy sauce
  • 🥢 6 tbsp oyster sauce
  • 🍷 6 tbsp cooking wine
  • 🌿 3 tsp Chinese 5 spice
  • 🧅 green onion
  • 🧄 garlic
  • 🥦 broccoli (approx. 1 head, or other veggie of choice)
  • 🥢 3 tsp sesame oil
  • 🫘 sesame seeds (optional)
  • Marinade:
    • 🫚 3 tsp ginger
    • 🥢 3 tbsp soy sauce
    • ☘️ 2 tsp black pepper
    • 🌽 2 tsp corn flour
    • 🧑‍🍳 1 1/2 tsp baking soda

Instructions

  1. Cut pork into very thin slices, mix and apply marinade, set aside.
  2. Mix sauce, chop veggies.
  3. In a large frying pan, begin by frying garlic until it begins to brown, then add marinated pork. Cook until pork is nearly done.
  4. Add sauce to pan, then add veggies.
  5. When the meat is fully cooked and the veggies have softened, add sesame oil and seeds if preferred.
  6. Serve with a side of rice.

entry.title: [ Blog ] Zucchini Pizza Casserole
entry.content:
Ingredients

  • 🥒 4 cups shredded unpeeled zucchini
  • 🥚 2 large eggs
  • 🧀 1/2 cup Parmesan
  • 🧀 2 cups mozzarella
  • 🧀 1 cup cheddar
  • 🐮 1 lbs ground beef
  • 🧅 1/2 cup onion
  • 🍅 1 can tomato sauce
  • 🫑 1 bell pepper

Instructions

  1. Preheat oven to 400 ℉. Shred zucchini and squeeze out moisture.
  2. Combine zucchini with the egg, and half of the cheese (Parmesan, mozzarella, and cheddar). Layer into the bottom of a large baking dish. Bake for 20 minutes
  3. Cook beef and onion completely in a saucepan, then add tomato sauce. Pour over the cooked egg layer, then sprinkle the remaining cheese on top. Bake for 20 more minutes until done.

Description

This is an italian-style caserole with pizza-like topping and a zuchini base. I first made it in 2023 and it tastes fantastic. I choose sometimes to skip the zuchini base to save time (or if I’m just being lazy). The topping is the signature feature of this dish, it really does taste like a pizza!
